accroche: An entire language was born on a playground, in less than two decades, without any adult teaching it or designing it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On a playground in Managua, in the very early 1980s, deaf children who had never shared a language began making one. No one taught it to them: it came out of their hands, between classes, and in less than two decades it had a grammar.

## A Language Without a Teacher

Before this period, deaf children in Nicaragua grew up isolated from one another. Each developed a personal gestural system with their family, what linguists call “homesign,” but these systems weren't passed from one child to another: no shared sign language existed in the country at the time. After the 1979 revolution, the government launched a literacy campaign and reopened a special education center in Managua, the Centro de Educación Especial Melania Morales, which brought together hundreds of deaf children for the first time. Official instruction there remained oral, lipreading and articulating Spanish, and had little success. But on the playground, on the bus, in the cafeteria, the children pooled their family gestures. A collective gestural communication emerged, without any adult designing or teaching it.

## From a Rough System to a Grammar

The first children brought together, often already teenagers, produced a functional but irregular system, close to what a linguist would call a pidgin. The younger children, who arrived afterward and grew up exposed very early to this still-unstable system, did not merely reproduce it. They regularized it, adding a coherent spatial grammar and verb agreement markers absent in their elders. In 1986, the Ministry of Education invited the American linguist Judy Kegl, trained at MIT, to observe the Managua schools; she filmed what would become the founding corpus for the study of this phenomenon. The linguist Ann Senghas continued the investigation in the 1990s by systematically comparing successive generations of students.

In a study published in 2001, Senghas and Marie Coppola measured the use of spatial grammar, the way of placing “characters” in signing space to indicate who does what to whom, among signers from different cohorts. The result is clear: those who joined the community before age 10 sign with a more systematic grammar than those who joined after that age, even though all of them today share the same linguistic environment. So it isn't merely exposure to the language that builds its grammar: it's the way young children rework it as they learn it.

## What This Shifts

We ordinarily imagine that a language is shaped over centuries, carried by generations of adult speakers. Nicaraguan Sign Language acquired a regular grammar in less than two decades, with no dictionary, no academy, and no teacher who knew it in advance, built largely by children under 10. It is an experiment that no ethics committee would allow anyone to provoke deliberately, and that a political revolution and a school reform made possible, unintentionally, just once.

repere.texte: Signers who joined the Managua deaf community before age 10 today sign with a markedly more systematic spatial grammar than those who joined after that age, although both groups have shared the same linguistic environment for decades.
repere.source: Ann Senghas and Marie Coppola, Psychological Science, 2001

carte.punch: An entire language was born on a playground, with no adult teaching it.
carte.idee: Deaf children in Nicaragua had no common language before 1979. Brought together in a school, they fashioned a gestural system that the youngest regularized into grammar. Learned before age 10, it is signed more systematically than when learned after that age.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Atlas Obscura — How Deaf Children in Nicaragua Created a New Language
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: An accessible account of the language's emergence, cohort by cohort.

quiz.question: What did the Senghas and Coppola study (2001) of Nicaraguan Sign Language make it possible to show?
choix: Children who learned the language before age 10 use a more systematic spatial grammar than those who learned it after age 10
All signers, whatever their age of learning, use exactly the same grammar, proving that age has no effect
Nicaraguan Sign Language actually derives from American Sign Language, brought by missionaries
Hearing children at the same school developed the same spatial grammar as the deaf children, through simple imitation
quiz.explication: Senghas and Coppola compare the use of spatial grammar between signers who joined the community before or after age 10: the former produce a markedly more regular grammar than the latter, even though they share the same linguistic environment today. Nicaraguan Sign Language has no lineage from ASL, and the effect is seen only among deaf signers who actively use it, not through simple surrounding imitation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before the late 1970s, how did deaf children in Nicaragua communicate, lacking a common language?
choix: By using a simplified version of American Sign Language
By all learning the same sign language in religious schools
Each with a personal gestural system, specific to their family
Through writing, with Spanish taught from the earliest age
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Each deaf child developed a personal gestural system with their family, a “homesign,” but these systems weren't passed from one child to another: no shared sign language existed in the country at the time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did deaf children in Nicaragua come to be brought together in numbers for the first time, in the early 1980s?
choix: During a national census organized by UNESCO
In a special education center reopened in Managua after the 1979 revolution
At a summer camp for disabled children, funded by an American NGO
At a national sign language competition
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After the 1979 revolution, the government launched a literacy campaign and reopened the Centro de Educación Especial Melania Morales in Managua, which brought together hundreds of deaf children for the first time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the generation of younger children, who arrived after the first teenagers brought together in Managua, do with the gestural system it finds already in place?
choix: It abandons it in favor of the lipreading taught at school
It reproduces it identically, without adding any new rule
It replaces it entirely with American Sign Language
It regularizes it, with a spatial grammar and verb agreement markers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The younger children don't merely reproduce the still-unstable system they find: they regularize it, adding a coherent spatial grammar and verb agreement markers absent in their elders.
